The bullet points show how the method ranked this transaction compared with the same address's transactions in the previous 14 days. The original plan used a fixed threshold that ranked transactions by how unusual they were compared with the same time in the previous 14 days. This gave a few flags every day, but the addresses would quickly become too crowded to review. So I changed it to a dynamic threshold that ranks transactions by how unusual they are compared with the same time in the previous 7 days. This gives fewer flags each day, and the addresses stay manageable.

The Explorer uses two public datasets: the Bitcoin blockchain snapshot from August 2017 (B) and the Bitcoin blockchain snapshot from May 2018 (M). The labels in B were created by analysts at the Anti-Fraud Analytics Lab at the University of Cambridge; those in M were created by the same team but retrained on a different dataset. Both sets contain thousands of labelled transactions, each with a score between 0 and 1, indicating how unusual the transaction was compared with that address's past.

Drift measures how far behind a method's answer is from the same method's answer on the same data, after a retrain. A method that stays close to itself has less drift than one that moves away. The Explorer uses drift as a way to compare methods: a method with less drift is better.

A small change can be unusual when compared with a much larger one. The Explorer uses z-scores to measure how far a value is from the usual value for that same direction. A z-score of 2 means the value is two usual spreads away from the usual value. A z-score of 5 would mean the value is five usual spreads away. The Explorer shows the three largest differences, and they are all at least 2 spread away from usual.

The Explorer uses a robust z-score method that does not depend on a global threshold: every feature has its own robust z-score, so a transaction can be unusual in one way and usual in another. This lets us say what stands out in the data itself, without assuming a global threshold.

TxGPT was trained on a snapshot of public Bitcoin blockchain data from May 2019, collected by the Blockstream Bitcoin research team. The snapshot contains over 1 billion transactions and 3 million addresses.

TxGPT is a small language model that predicts whether a transaction happened by itself or was part of a sequence. It works by comparing each transaction with the address's recent history: transactions that look similar are likely to have happened one after the other. The Explorer uses it to say whether a gap between transactions is unusually long, and whether a gap ends with a transaction that looks different from the rest.

DBSCAN finds dense groups of transactions and labels the rest as noise. A transaction is dense if most of its neighbours are also in the same group. The distance between two transactions is how far apart their gaps are on a timeline.

Size is the amount of the transaction, in BTC. The Explorer uses that number as a baseline for comparison with the address's usual pattern.
Relative size compares the amount with the address's usual amount for that direction (received or sent). A large received amount far above the usual amount would be unusual, but so would a small sent amount far below the usual one.

Regression measures how the size and direction of a transaction differ from what the address usually has. A transaction far outside the usual range is unusual. A Burst is a way to compare a transaction with the address's usual pattern over the previous 14 days. A transaction far outside the usual range is flagged as unusual. The Explorer uses bursts from 2 to 14 days ago; earlier ones would show a longer history than the snapshot used for classification.

The z number measures how unusual a value is compared with that address's usual pattern. A z of 2 or more means the value is far outside the usual range, much farther than 95% of similar values would be. A z of 1 or less means the value is close to usual; a transaction in the usual direction would be far more usual.

K-Means groups transactions into a few typical patterns, called clusters. It finds those patterns by making guesses about where they are, and then moving them around until the whole collection fits together nicely. The Explorer uses K-Means to find the usual way an address works, and then compares each transaction with that usual way.

A flag measures how far a feature's value is from what the address usually has: the usual value plus or minus three usual spreads. A flag means that one feature is far from usual; a robust z of 2 or more means that two features are far from usual. The Explorer uses these methods with the same data that trained the models, so a flag measures how different a transaction is from what the address usually does.
